# Clinical Vignette: Fatima

Fatima, a 69-year-old woman of Syrian descent, has worked the morning shift at a fast-food restaurant in suburban Ohio for the past twelve years. Her routine has always steadied her—arriving at 5 a.m. to prep the grill, moving through the familiar motions until the lunch crowd thinned. But the woman who arrives at that restaurant now is not the woman who did so three years ago, before the man began to follow her.

She first noticed him in the parking lot of a grocery store near her home, a man in his fifties with a silver sedan. He smiled at her in a way that felt deliberate, held her gaze too long. She left quickly. Two days later, she saw him again—this time parked outside the restaurant during her shift, watching through the glass. When she mentioned it to her husband, he suggested she was being oversensitive. But the man returned, and then again, always watching, sometimes writing things in a notebook. For eight months, he appeared and disappeared from her life like a recurring nightmare. He learned her schedule, waited for her in different locations, once approached her at a gas station and said he knew where she lived. She reported him to police, who filed a report but found no basis for charges. He was simply being "persistent," they said. Then one morning, he did not appear, and he has not been seen since. But he lives inside Fatima now, and he has not left.

The relief she expected to feel never came. Instead, something fragmented. In the three years since his disappearance, Fatima has become someone she does not recognize. She lies awake most nights, her eyes opening at 2 a.m., 3 a.m., sometimes every hour, seized by the need to verify that the front door is locked, that the garage door is closed, that the windows are secure. Her husband hears her moving through the house in darkness, and he has stopped asking her to come back to bed. She checks the locks again before she leaves for work, and again when she returns, sometimes five or six times in an evening, her hand on the deadbolt, turning it, testing it, turning it again. The ritual brings no peace.

At the restaurant, everything has become a calculation of threat. She studies the faces of customers as they approach the counter, reading their expressions for intention, scanning their body language for signs of aggression or obsession. A man who lingers too long at the menu board sets her heart racing. A customer who orders the same thing twice in one week triggers a cascade of fear. She has memorized the faces of regulars, watching for any shift in their attention toward her, any pattern that might suggest interest. Her coworkers have noticed her withdrawal, the way she flinches when someone approaches from behind. The manager has gently suggested that she might consider a different shift, one with fewer customer interactions. She is considering it, though the thought of changing her routine—the one reliable thing in a life that no longer feels like her own—terrifies her in a different way.

The memories of those eight months arrive without warning and with a clarity that feels impossible. Sometimes she smells his cologne, a sharp cologne with a woody undertone, and for a moment she is certain he is there in the room with her, even though she knows he is not. Other times, she can recount the sequence of events—the parking lot, the gas station, the way he said he knew where she lived—but the experience feels as though it happened to someone else, as though she is narrating a story from a film she once watched. The extremity of it, the sustained nature of his attention, the way he had woven himself into her daily life: it all feels too surreal to have actually happened to her. She wonders sometimes if she imagined parts of it, if she made it worse in her mind.

What frightens her most now is not the man, who is gone, but the possibility that she will lose the ability to manage her own fear. She has come to believe that if she allows herself to think deeply about what happened, to truly face it, she will collapse entirely. She has also come to believe something darker: that people cannot be trusted, that the world contains predators who move through it freely, and that safety is an illusion. She looks at her husband of forty-five years and sometimes wonders if she ever really knew him. She looks at herself in the mirror and does not recognize the woman looking back—vigilant, guarded, exhausted. Her daughter, visiting from Michigan last month, held her hand and asked when her mother was going to get help. Fatima has finally called a therapist. She is terrified that facing this will break her. She is also terrified of what she has already become.
